cases.answer: I'd write async function fetchJson<T>(url: string): Promise<Result<T>> where type Result<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string }. The generic parameter T is given at the call site, for example fetchJson<User>('/api/user'), and it flows through to the data field of the result. The ok property is a literal true or false, so it is the discriminant of the union. Inside I await fetch in a try/catch; on a non-2xx response or a thrown error I return ok false with an error message. At the call site I check if (result.ok) and only inside that branch TypeScript lets me read result.data; in the else branch only result.error exists. There is no any anywhere: the parsed JSON is typed as T or unknown.

The result type is a union of two shapes, one with ok set to the literal true plus the data, one with ok set to the literal false plus an error string; that literal is what TypeScript discriminates on. When the caller writes fetchJson<Order[]>(...) the type argument travels into the return type, so data comes back as Order[]. The function is async, awaits the request inside try and catch, and turns network failures or bad status codes into the error variant. Because of the discriminant, data is only reachable after checking that ok is true. I avoid the any type completely and use unknown before narrowing.

The generic parameter T is given at the call site and flows through to the data field. The ok property is a literal true or false, so it is the discriminant. Inside I await fetch in a try/catch and return ok false on errors. Narrowing works because TypeScript checks the ok property at runtime and throws if data is missing, so after if (result.ok) data is safe. There is no any anywhere.

Generics are really powerful in TypeScript. You make a helper that is generic and returns a result, and then TypeScript just knows all the types, so everything is type safe and clean. It's a best practice that makes the code robust, scalable and maintainable, and it's what senior engineers do.

For a browser app I'd use cookie sessions. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt or argon2, which add a per-password salt; they are never stored in plain text. The session cookie is httpOnly so scripts can't read it, secure so it only travels over HTTPS, and sameSite lax or strict. JWTs with short-lived access tokens and refresh token rotation avoid server state, but revoking them is hard until they expire, and that is the trade-off. Cookies expose you to CSRF, which sameSite and CSRF tokens handle, while tokens kept in localStorage are exposed to XSS. OAuth and OpenID Connect delegate login to an identity provider; they are not a way to store passwords.

Stored passwords go through a slow salted hash such as argon2 or bcrypt. With sessions, the browser holds a cookie flagged httpOnly, secure and sameSite. JWT access tokens expire quickly and are renewed with rotating refresh tokens, which saves a session store but makes instant revocation difficult. The main risk with cookies is cross-site request forgery, with tokens in script-readable storage it is cross-site scripting. OpenID Connect and OAuth are about handing authentication to another provider, not about storing credentials. For a normal web app I'd pick sessions.

The input value becomes a stream: I apply debounceTime(300) and then switchMap to the API call, so a new keystroke cancels the stale request. I convert the result stream into a signal with toSignal(), which is the RxJS interop function, and the template reads that signal. The result count is a computed() derived from the results signal. I'd avoid effects except for side jobs like logging, because they make the data flow harder to follow.

Template state lives in signals: the results come from toSignal() over the search observable, which is how the RxJS interop bridges the two worlds, and the number shown is a computed() over that signal. The observable side handles timing: debounceTime waits for typing to pause and switchMap drops any request that is still in flight when a newer term arrives. Effects are kept to a minimum.

Signals are the modern way and RxJS is the old way, so I would mostly use signals because they are simpler and faster, and only use RxJS where it really makes sense. That gives a clean, reactive and performant architecture.
